rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Brewster's angle, where n = tan i_p, fully polarises the reflected light, and the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular. A Polaroid selects one transverse direction, and Malus' law gives I_0 cos^2 θ for a second Polaroid. Crossed axes pass nothing.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Unpolarised through one Polaroid: intensity about half.  ·  i_p is often near 57° for glass.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Light is a transverse electromagnetic wave. Its electric field can point in any direction in the plane perpendicular to the ray. Polarised light has that field along one line.  ·  At Brewster's angle of incidence, the reflected light is completely plane polarised. The refractive index and that angle are related by n = tan i_p.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Polarisation is a transverse-wave fact.  ·  Brewster's angle gives full polarisation of the reflected ray.  ·  At that angle the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular.  ·  A Polaroid passes one direction.

rows.label: Universal facts

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Glass has n = 1.50. Find Brewster's angle, then the intensity fraction through a second Polaroid at 60° to the first if the light reaching it is polarised. Use tan 56° ≈ 1.48.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: At the same angle the reflected ray and the refracted ray are at 90° to each other. That geometry is why the reflected electric field has only one direction left.  ·  A Polaroid has long molecules that absorb one component and pass the perpendicular component. Two Polaroids with their axes at angle θ pass intensity I_0 cos^2 θ if the incident light is already polarised. That is Malus' law.  ·  Crossed Polaroids, θ = 90°, pass no light. Parallel Polaroids pass the full polarised intensity. Unpolarised light through one Polaroid loses half its intensity, because half the components are absorbed.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Brewster's law is n = tan i_p, not sin i_p.  ·  Malus uses the square of the cosine.  ·  Crossed Polaroids transmit nothing.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: One Polaroid on unpolarised light transmits about half, not all.  ·  Use tan, not sin.  ·  Square the cosine in Malus.
